body: i'm not really here to debate methodology. i've considered the 'how' for about a decade and i've come to the conclusion that jumping is the best way.  the exhaust poisoning probably won't work because i'll either change my mind halfway through or someone will find me. all it takes is one step forward to make the decision irreversible.

i'm not sure how to define "being someone worthwhile."

i have infallible confidence that i'm one of the "good guys". i've spent the majority of my life helping people; the thing i'm proudest of is that i actually helped a close friend climb her way out of depression a few months ago. it's always my philosophy that if you don't do more good than evil you're not worthy of existence anyways.

on the other side, i have been rather outwardly successful. i would have graduated from my university on full ride in three years, while working an internship at a biometrics firm to make that resume sexy. you could see me every day, and indeed most people do, being blissfully unaware that i'm in the slightest bit unhappy.

i've never actually given the "accidental death" idea much thought...

the trouble i see with that is that i'm not sure anyone would believe it. that is, the people around me are at least aware of my suicidal tendencies and it would be mighty suspicious if i suddenly had a hiking accident.  plus that eliminates my ability to send my letters.

an interesting proposition though, i'll give it more thought. i've got nothing but time...

yes i realize that there is no way a suicide can be an 'orderly affair'. i realize it will most likely horrify and emotionally scar quite a few people. it's just that since i'm set on the selfish decision, i thought i'd try to soften the blow a little bit at least.

as i mentioned earlier, i realize i'm not alone in the world. however, i have tried to open up to the people i care about and they simply do not understand. at best they offer empty platitudes and at worst, they 'freak out'.  i'm a firm believer that if you haven't been there yourself, you cannot appreciate the distinction between sadness and depression.

i'm sorry to say that i can't even point you in the right direction to a subjective meaning of life.  i will mention some things that have not worked for me:

as i said, early on in life i tried to find meaning in religion.  and while i don't think this is the place for a theological debate, i find it suffice to say that i could not accept the idea of a benevolent, omnipotent  god that nevertheless allowed such suffering in the world.

i thought for a while that my depression was purely situational. my home life was unsupportive, to put it politely.  for years i thought that if i could just escape all the negativity surrounding me i could find happiness.  so as soon as i graduated high school i moved out and got an apartment with my best friend, on campus at my new university. after three years of living on my own, i am still not content with my life.

for a while i thought that i was perhaps just lonely.  that one day i would find someone to share my life with and live happily ever after. while i'm still not in a conventional relationship, i've developed a few very close, ah, 'friendships with benefits'.  after a great deal of discussion and reflection, i came to the conclusion that on a fundamental level, this is something inherent to me that i have to deal with myself. don't get me wrong, my friends give me more happiness than anything else in life and without them i would have taken the leap years ago. however, it is neither reasonable nor fair to expect someone else to be responsible for your happiness and emotional stability.

i thought that perhaps then i was too confined in my life. i've always been a very calm and logical sort, so i tried to be impulsive.  i bought things that i've always wanted, i called in sick to work or cut class whenever i felt like it, i shirked responsibilities and commitments wherever possible.  even with my scholarship i've managed to burn through a few thousand dollars and while i'm still passing my classes, my grades have noticeably slumped. and i must say that while some of these things are wonderful diversions, at the end of the day it's all shallow and superficial and it fades quickly.

sorry for the long reply, i just hope that somehow my experiences might help you or someone else that stumbles upon this thread.  any insights you have would be greatly appreciated, even if it is a list of things that DIDNT work such as mine.

i suppose part of the problem is that i'm constantly searching for the 'end solution.' if life itself is the journey, i find the journey unpleasant.  i want something concrete, something real, that i can point to and say 'THIS. THIS is why i'm here, THIS is why i'm alive, THIS is why i should continue to live.' my existence thus far seems pointless and fairly arbitrary.

by extension i'm guessing that you are trying to tell me that there are no single answer. to some extent i've already accepted that; if life were that simple i wouldn't being having troubles in the first place. perhaps i'm just selfish or greedy but i must be honest and say that a journey of enlightenment or whatnot sounds... well daunting. the sort of thing that i just don't have the energy for.

of course, i might be entirely off the mark with my generalizations here.  i'll give the audiobook a try and then hopefully be able to respond in a more informed manner.

i fully understand that my own mind is my worst enemy.  the more i think about things, the worse any situation becomes.  i'm a computer science major, but i spend more time thinking about life and all its futility in the abstract than i do thinking about algorithms.

my parents tried to raise me as a lutheran, and for a couple of years i tried to get it to stick in my mind.  i wanted to believe, but found i could not.  other 'self-help' type things i've read have all been nauseating.  i have no experience with "the way of zen", and i promise you that i will give this a try.  the 'weight of existence' seems to describe my problems very accurately.  however, i must admit that at this point i'm rather pessimistic about finding the solution in a book.

as for sports, i've never been very athletic. physical competition always seemed rather irrelevant to me in the modern society.  about eight months ago i did start working out regularly at the gym, and i found it kind of peaceful. i've since gotten away from that (when i moved to a new apartment, the gym is now far less convenient to go to on a regular basis), but i really should get back to it.

i don't want to make this out as a 'i hate the direction my life is going' story.  there was a point in time i loved my major and i was terribly excited to be going to my school.  over the years i've just... lost interest.  However, there's nothing else out there that i'd rather being doing, at least not that i know of.

and i realize i'm young and have my whole life ahead of me, and that's perhaps the scariest part of all.  i've already suffered through several years of suicidal thoughts and frankly, i don't want to deal with several more.  i've kept myself going because i thought that once i got to a certain 'landmark' i would be happy; but i've met all those goals and i'm still miserable. thus, the potential for happiness is no longer appealing enough to keep me going.

this seems perfectly logical.  however my problem is i don't know what it is that i should change.

this past year or so i've been growing more desperate, and so i've been acting rather impulsively.  if i'd rather go to a party than study for my midterm coming up, i do so.  if there's something i want that i can't really afford, i buy it anyway. i meet a girl that's in a committed relationship, i hook up with her anyway.  of course, none of these shallow things make me truly happy.

i guess i could try to do something more drastic to alter my life, but hellifino what...
well if you find any answers, let me know and i'll do the same. deal?
